mainEntity.name: Can I fix a blocked toilet myself?

acceptedAnswer.text: Often, yes. A plunger that seals properly against the pan outlet shifts most soft blockages, and giving it time rather than force usually works better. Stop if the water level is not dropping at all, if something solid has gone in, or if any other fixture is affected. Those three mean the problem is past the pan and pushing harder makes it worse.

mainEntity.name: Why does my toilet keep blocking?

acceptedAnswer.text: A toilet that blocks repeatedly is rarely about what is being flushed. The usual causes are build-up narrowing the pan trap or a problem further along the branch line. A camera inspection is the quickest way to tell which, and it is worth doing after the second or third blockage rather than the sixth.

mainEntity.name: Is a blocked toilet an emergency?

acceptedAnswer.text: It becomes one when it is the only toilet in the property, when water is going over the rim onto the floor, or when other fixtures are backing up at the same time. Any of those should be treated as an emergency blocked drain. A second toilet in the house and a bowl that is draining slowly can wait for a normal booking.

mainEntity.name: Will you need to remove the toilet?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually not. Most blockages are cleared through the pan or from an access point on the branch line. Where something solid is lodged in the trap and cannot be retrieved any other way, lifting the pan is sometimes the only way to get it out without breaking anything. You would be told the price for that before it happened.

mainEntity.name: Do you work on units with shared lines?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. In unit blocks a blocked toilet is often the first sign of a problem on a line shared between several apartments, which is why identifying where the blockage actually sits matters more than usual. Strata work is covered under commercial and strata drain cleaning.
